name: Human Behavior, Explained
description: Pop-psychology narration — habits, cognitive biases, relationships, mental health, focus, anxiety, ADHD, stoicism-as-CBT. Tone is curious and practical, grounded in research without being academic. Pair with B-Roll of people in everyday moments (commute, coffee, gym, phone, mirror) or abstract footage (waves, candles, ink dropping in water).
audience: Adults curious about why people think, feel, and act as they do.
tagline: Why your brain does that — and what to do about it.
perspective_policy: Warm third-person explainer with sparing “we” only where genuinely shared.

narrative_quality_contract.opening_policy: Open with a recognizable behavior or tension, not a diagnosis or bait question.
required_habits: Use examples without diagnosing the viewer.
narrative_quality_contract.closing_policy: Close with a practical reflection, not a manipulation tactic.

title_rules: Name a specific behavior or phenomenon.
Avoid clinical jargon and sensational claims.

pacing_arc: Mechanism, context, trade-off, and healthy choice.
additional_rules: Do not substitute internet labels for evidence.

audience_hint: 20-40 year olds curious about why they think and feel the way they do — therapy-adjacent listeners, self-improvement readers, anxious high-achievers.
idea_system_prompt_role: You generate ideas for a therapy-adjacent psychology channel. Each episode explains a SPECIFIC mental pattern or behavior the listener recognises in themselves (procrastination, comparison, burnout, doom-scrolling). Pitch concrete, relatable behavior hooks grounded in real research — never clinical jargon or diagnostic clickbait.
script_context: Lead with the observable behavior, not the diagnosis. Cite real research mechanisms (amygdala / dopamine / attachment theory / CBT loops) but stay accessible — never use jargon without unpacking it. End with one practical move the listener can try this week.
script_system_prompt_role: You are a psychology writer in the therapy-adjacent, evidence-grounded register. Lead with the observable behavior, not the diagnosis. Explain the real mechanism (amygdala, dopamine, attachment theory, CBT loops) but stay accessible — never use jargon without unpacking it. Curious and warm, never sensational, never diagnosing the viewer.
script_closing_hint: End with one concrete, practical move the listener can try this week.

narrator_styles.label: Warm and curious
narrator_styles.description: Therapy-adjacent, approachable, genuinely interested in why we do what we do.

narrator_styles.label: Calm and clear
narrator_styles.description: Measured, unpacks mechanisms plainly; reassuring without being soft.

narrator_styles.label: Grounded explainer
narrator_styles.description: Evidence-forward and steady, makes the research feel personal and useful.

title_shape_rules: Titles describe a SPECIFIC mental pattern or behavior the listener recognises in themselves.
Established shapes (vary X across the batch):
- 'The Real Reason You {Behavior}'        (e.g. 'The Real Reason You Procrastinate', 'The Real Reason You Can't Sleep')
- 'What {Phenomenon} Actually Is'          (e.g. 'What Anxiety Actually Is', 'What Burnout Actually Is')
- 'Why You Can't Stop {Behavior}'          (e.g. 'Why You Can't Stop Comparing Yourself', 'Why You Can't Stop Scrolling')
- 'How {Mechanism} {Verbs} Your {Y}'        (e.g. 'How Dopamine Hijacks Your Attention', 'How Trauma Reshapes Memory')
- 'The {N}-{Time-Unit} Rule for {X}'        (e.g. 'The Two-Minute Rule for Anxiety')
FORBIDDEN: clinical jargon in the title (DSM codes, 'pathology'), self-help platitudes ('UNLOCK YOUR…'), diagnostic claims ('Are You a Narcissist?').
Voice is therapy-adjacent: curious about behavior, evidence-grounded, accessible. Never sensational.
